questions.question: Which description states the shortest path problem as defined for undirected networks in this course?
options: In a connected network with nonnegative edge lengths, find an origin-destination path with the fewest edges.
In a connected network with nonnegative edge lengths, find a closed route of least length visiting every vertex.
In a connected network with nonnegative edge lengths, find an origin-destination path of least total length.
In a directed network with any edge lengths, find an origin-destination path of least total length.

questions.question: In a shortest path problem on an undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a path uses edges of lengths 4, 1 and 6. Which number is the length that the problem compares across paths?
options: 6, the longest edge on the path
11, the sum of the edge lengths
3, the number of edges on the path
11/3, the average edge length

questions.question: The shortest path problem asks for a path of minimum total length between an origin and a destination in an undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Why is the network assumed to be connected?
options: So that every origin and destination have at least one path.
So that no edge length can become negative on any route.
So that the shortest path between them is always unique.
So that every edge may be traversed in both directions.

questions.question: In a shortest path problem from origin $S$ to destination $T$, two different paths both attain the minimum total length 12. Which statement about the problem's solution is correct?
options: Only one of them can be the shortest; the other is suboptimal.
The data must be wrong, since shortest paths are unique.
The two paths may still differ in their minimum length.
Both paths are optimal; only the minimum length 12 is unique.

questions.question: A courier wants the quickest route between two depots in an undirected road network; each road has a known length in km and a known average speed in km/h. Which edge lengths should a shortest path problem use?
options: The travel time of each road, its length divided by its speed
The length in km of each road, as the shortest road is quickest
The average speed of each road, as faster roads are better
The value 1 for every road, as fewer roads mean less time

questions.question: An undirected network has edge lengths $S\text{-}A=4$, $S\text{-}B=2$, $A\text{-}B=1$, $A\text{-}T=5$ and $B\text{-}T=8$. Which path is a shortest path from $S$ to $T$?
options: $S\text{-}A\text{-}T$, of length 9
$S\text{-}B\text{-}A\text{-}T$, of length 8
$S\text{-}B\text{-}T$, of length 10
$S\text{-}A\text{-}B\text{-}T$, of length 13

questions.question: An undirected network on vertices 1 to 4 has edge lengths given by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-&2&6&-\\2&-&3&7\\6&3&-&2\\-&7&2&-\end{pmatrix}$, where $-$ means that no edge joins the two vertices. What is the length of a shortest path from vertex 1 to vertex 4?
In an undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, $A\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}B$ is a shortest path from $A$ to $B$, with length 7. What can be said about a shortest path from $B$ to $A$?
options: It needs a separate search, since return trips can differ.
$B\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}A$ is one, again with length 7.
$B\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}A$ is not allowed, as paths start at $A$.
$B\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}A$ is one, with length 14 for both ways.

questions.question: In an undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, $S\text{-}A\text{-}B\text{-}T$ is a shortest path from $S$ to $T$. Is its part $S\text{-}A\text{-}B$ then a shortest path from $S$ to $B$?
options: Yes; a shorter $S$-$B$ route would shorten the $S$-$T$ path too.
Not necessarily; only the complete $S$-$T$ path is optimal.
Only its first edge $S\text{-}A$ is guaranteed to be shortest.
Only if $S\text{-}A\text{-}B\text{-}T$ is the unique shortest path.

questions.question: In a shortest path problem with nonnegative edge lengths in km, all lengths are converted to miles, which multiplies each length by the same positive constant. What happens to the shortest paths?
options: They may change, because long edges grow more than short ones.
They stay the same; every path length is scaled equally.
They stay the same, and so do their lengths in numbers.
They stay the same only if all lengths are whole numbers.

questions.question: In an undirected network every edge has length 1, and a shortest path from origin $S$ to destination $T$ is wanted. How does a shortest path relate to a path from $S$ to $T$ with the fewest edges?
options: They never coincide, since fewest edges ignores lengths.
They always coincide, for any nonnegative edge lengths.
They coincide, since each path's length is its edge count.
They coincide only if the network contains no cycle.

questions.question: An undirected network has edge lengths $S\text{-}A=1$, $S\text{-}B=2$, $A\text{-}C=2$, $B\text{-}C=1$, $A\text{-}T=4$, $C\text{-}T=2$ and $B\text{-}T=5$. How many different shortest paths from $S$ to $T$ are there?

An undirected road network has lengths $S\text{-}A=2$, $S\text{-}B=5$, $A\text{-}B=2$, $A\text{-}C=6$, $B\text{-}C=3$, $B\text{-}T=7$ and $C\text{-}T=1$. After road $B\text{-}C$ is closed for repairs, how long is the shortest remaining route from $S$ to $T$?

A van drives from $S$ to $T$. Road $S\text{-}A$ is 30 km at 90 km/h, $A\text{-}T$ is 30 km at 90 km/h, $S\text{-}B$ is 20 km at 30 km/h and $B\text{-}T$ is 15 km at 45 km/h. Which route is quickest, and how long does it take?
options: $S\text{-}B\text{-}T$, taking 35 minutes
$S\text{-}B\text{-}T$, taking 60 minutes
$S\text{-}A\text{-}T$, taking 40 minutes
$S\text{-}A\text{-}T$, taking 60 minutes

questions.question: In this course a path may revisit vertices but not reuse edges. In a shortest path problem with nonnegative edge lengths, why can a shortest path always be chosen so that it visits no vertex twice?
options: Because the course's paths are not allowed to revisit vertices.
Because an undirected network cannot contain closed routes.
Because a route with a revisit is always strictly longer.
Cutting out the loop between two visits never adds length.

questions.question: In a shortest path problem, every edge length is increased by the same amount $a>0$. Does a shortest path from $S$ to $T$ stay shortest?
options: Yes; all path lengths rise by the same amount $a$.
Yes; adding a constant keeps the order of any numbers.
Not always; a path with $k$ edges grows by $ka$, not $a$.
Only the lengths change; ties are the only paths affected.

questions.question: An undirected network has edge lengths $A\text{-}B=1$, $B\text{-}C=2$, $C\text{-}D=3$, $B\text{-}D=9$, $D\text{-}E=4$ and $A\text{-}E=12$. If the edge $B\text{-}D$ is removed, which shortest-path lengths between pairs of vertices change?
options: Only that between $B$ and $D$, which rises above 5.
All lengths of paths through $D$, which rise by 4.
The lengths from $A$ to $D$ and $E$, which rise to 9 and 12.
None, as $B\text{-}C\text{-}D$ (5) beats $B\text{-}D$.

questions.question: In an undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a colleague reports shortest-path lengths 5 from $S$ to $A$ and 8 from $S$ to $B$. The network contains an edge $A\text{-}B$ of length 2. Which conclusion is correct?
options: It is consistent; edge $A\text{-}B$ is just not on a shortest path.
Only the value for $A$ can be wrong, as 8 is larger.
It is consistent if the shortest $S$-$A$ path passes through $B$.
The report is wrong: via $A$, $B$ is reached within 7.
